public_rationale: Ramp reports median monthly AI spending of $11.95 per employee in its sample for July 2026 [e1]. This supports modest spending for the typical sampled firm, but does not establish the spending of a vast majority of enterprises [e1]. Morning Consult's July 2026 survey measures plans to increase spending over the next 12 months, not actual expenditure [e2]. These measurements do not settle the population-wide claim [e1] [e2].
limitations: The evidence lacks a representative July 2026 spending distribution covering enterprises generally and AI purchases across providers.
The sampled median does not establish spending throughout the upper half or spending relative to software budgets.
The claim defines no numerical threshold for 'vast majority' or modest spending.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The vast majority of enterprises do not spend much money on AI.

statement.excerpt: This means that the vast majority of enterprises — which is where the real money is in software — just don’t spend that much money on AI.

from_speaker: just don’t spend that much money on AI
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that a large majority of businesses spend modest amounts on AI relative to their size and ordinary software budgets.
Spending less than a few exceptionally large customers does not by itself establish modest spending.
Use July 2026, the latest monthly spending period in the pre-publication Ramp report located during source verification.
No numerical definition of modest spending or vast majority is added.
The aside about software revenue is contextual rather than a separate quantitative claim.
criteria.support_condition: Representative spending distributions show that a large majority of enterprises have modest AI expenditure relative to their size or software budgets.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative spending distributions show that substantial AI expenditure is common enough to rule out the claimed large majority with modest spending.
